title: Sometimes What You Need Is Right in Front of You
author: Thomas O'Brien
source: How Math Saves the World (howmathsavestheworld.substack.com), November 14, 2026
summary: O'Brien, a former math teacher and author of a book on math leadership, argues that school leaders already have powerful instructional resources sitting unused in state guidance. He opens with two stories from his own career: studying a district portal of past state exam questions turned his struggling first-year results into the district's biggest gains, and scoring state math exams showed him exactly how points are won and lost. He then surveys what New Mexico and Texas have published, including math frameworks, instructional scope documents, leadership guides and classroom look-fors, and asks how many principals have actually studied them. The real work of school leadership, he says, is translating that guidance into observations, coaching conversations, teacher development and priorities. He closes with five Monday-ready steps, from finding the state framework to using it to advocate for funding and professional learning.
points: O'Brien's own gains came from using resources available to everyone, a district exam-question portal and state exam scoring, which shows that aligning instruction to what students are expected to demonstrate can be a near silver bullet.
States such as New Mexico and Texas have already published frameworks, instructional scope documents, leadership guides and look-fors, so the gap is awareness and use rather than availability.

School leaders add value by translating state guidance into classroom observations, coaching conversations and teacher development, for example by asking whether Algebra I teachers routinely have students explain why a procedure works.
Aligning the school improvement plan with state expectations also strengthens funding and PD requests and builds a shared language across the leadership team.
He offers five starting moves, including finding the state framework, locating look-fors and coaching guides, and studying the materials with a strong math teacher or department chair.
quotes: Twice in my teaching career, I found state/district provided resources that helped me improve student outcomes without having to reinvent my instruction. Both were available to me and everyone else but only a few took advantage.

I saw where students earned points, where they lost them, and the different ways they approached the same problems. I could see the difference between students who understood the math but failed to communicate their thinking clearly and those who demonstrated strong reasoning, even when they made a computational error.

States have invested significant time, research, and resources into defining strong math instruction and developing tools to support it. The question is how many school leaders know these resources exist, have studied them, and are using them to guide their work each day.

A state can define high-quality math instruction, recommend strong curriculum materials, and establish expectations for professional learning. But someone (you!) at the school needs to translate those recommendations into classroom observations, coaching conversations, teacher development, and instructional priorities.
That’s a helpful reminder, but what does that actually look like in your Algebra I classrooms? Are teachers routinely asking students to explain why a procedure works?

Beyond improving coaching, understanding your state's expectations can help align your school improvement plan, strengthen requests for funding and professional learning, and create a shared language for math instruction across your leadership team.
Look beyond the academic standards and identify how your state defines high-quality math instruction. Compare that vision with what you are seeing in your classrooms.
Start by finding out what your state has already developed. Study it. Talk about it with your teachers.
context: Both of his career turning points came from tools every teacher in the district could have used.
Scoring state exams showed him the difference between understanding and communicating understanding.
He reframes the problem for leaders as one of awareness and use of existing state resources.
This is his definition of the school leader's job: turning guidance into daily practice.
A concrete example of a framework principle turned into an observation question.

The first of his five starting steps is to compare the state's definition of good instruction with classrooms.
